{{short description|Theorem on edge-disjoint spanning trees}}
In [[graph theory]], the '''Nash-Williams theorem''' is a '''[[tree-packing]]''' theorem that describes how many edge-disjoint [[spanning tree]]s (and more generally [[Forest (graph theory)|forests]]) a graph can have:
<blockquote>A graph ''G'' has ''t'' edge-disjoint spanning trees iff for every partition <math display="inline">V_1, \ldots, V_k \subset V(G)</math> where <math>V_i \neq \emptyset</math> there are at least ''t''(''k''&nbsp;−&nbsp;1) crossing edges.
</blockquote>
The theorem was proved independently by [[W. T. Tutte|Tutte]]<ref name="t61">{{cite journal |last1=Tutte |first1=W. T. |title=On the problem of decomposing a graph into <math>n</math> connected factors|journal=Journal of the London Mathematical Society |date=1961 |volume=36 |issue=1 |pages=221-230 |doi=10.1112/jlms/s1-36.1.221}}</ref> and [[Crispin Nash-Williams|Nash-Williams]],<ref name="nw61">{{cite journal |last1=Nash-Williams |first1=Crispin St. John Alvah |title=Edge-Disjoint Spanning Trees of Finite Graphs |journal=Journal of the London Mathematical Society |date=1961 |volume=36 |issue=1 |pages=445–450 |doi=10.1112/jlms/s1-36.1.445}}</ref> both in 1961. In 2012, Kaiser<ref name="k12">{{cite journal |last1=Kaiser |first1=Tomáš |title=A short proof of the tree-packing theorem |journal=Discrete Mathematics |date=2012 |volume=312 |issue=10 |pages=1689-1691 |doi=10.1016/j.disc.2012.01.020 |arxiv=0911.2809}}</ref> gave a short elementary proof. 

For this article, we say that such a graph has '''arboricity&nbsp;''t''''' or is ''t''-'''arboric'''. (The actual definition of [[arboricity]] is slightly different and applies to forests rather than trees.)

== Related tree-packing properties ==
A ''k''-arboric graph is necessarily [[K-edge-connected graph|''k''-edge connected]]. The converse is not true.

As a corollary of the Nash-Williams theorem, every 2''k''-edge connected graph is ''k''-arboric.

Both Nash-Williams' theorem and [[Menger's theorem]] characterize when a graph has ''k'' edge-disjoint paths between two vertices.

== Nash-Williams theorem for forests ==
In 1964, Nash-Williams<ref name=nw64>{{cite journal |last1=Nash-Williams |first1=Crispin St. John Alvah |title=Decomposition of Finite Graphs Into Forests |journal=Journal of the London Mathematical Society |date=1964 |volume=39 |issue=1 |page=12 |doi=10.1112/jlms/s1-39.1.12}}</ref> generalized the above result to forests:<blockquote>A graph <math>G</math> can be partitioned into <math>t</math> edge-disjoint forests iff for every <math>U \subset V(G)</math>, the [[induced subgraph]] <math>G[U]</math> has at most <math>t(|U|-1)</math> edges. </blockquote>Other proofs are given here.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Chen|first1=Boliong|last2=Matsumoto|first2=Makoto|last3=Wang|first3=Jianfang|last4=Zhang|first4=Zhongfu|last5=Zhang|first5=Jianxun|date=1994-03-01|title=A short proof of Nash-Williams' theorem for the arboricity of a graph|journal=Graphs and Combinatorics|language=en|volume=10|issue=1|pages=27–28|doi=10.1007/BF01202467|s2cid=206791653 |issn=1435-5914}}</ref><ref name="d17">{{Cite book|title=Graph theory|last=Diestel|first= Reinhard|isbn=9783662536216|oclc=1048203362|date = 2017-06-30}}</ref>

This is how people usually define what it means for a graph to be '''''t''-arboric.'''

In other words, for every subgraph <math>S=G[U]</math>, we have <math>t \geq \lceil E(S) / (V(S) - 1) \rceil</math>. It is tight in that there is a subgraph <math>S</math> that saturates the inequality (or else we can choose a smaller <math>t</math>). This leads to the following formula<blockquote><math>t = \lceil \max_{S \subset G} \frac{E(S)}{V(S) - 1} \rceil</math>,</blockquote>also referred to as the '''Nash-Williams formula.'''

The general problem is to ask when a graph can be covered by edge-disjoint subgraphs.
